title: Support Selective Loss Evaluation for Partial Annotations / Multi-Dataset Training
body:
We have a scenario in our object detection training pipeline where not every image sample is fully annotated for all possible classes. This situation happens when combining multiple datasets (e.g., COCO along with other datasets), where each dataset may only include labels for a subset of classes. If the model is trained without any modifications, unannotated classes in a sample would be incorrectly treated as negatives, leading to suboptimal gradient updates.

Proposed Solution:
Introduce an extra per-sample property (or mask) that explicitly lists which classes are annotated (or should be evaluated) for that sample. During training, the loss function would use this mask to selectively backpropagate only for the annotated classes. This approach would allow us to:
	•	Train on multiple datasets with partially overlapping class labels.
	•	Prevent the model from being penalized for missing annotations.
	•	Use the combined knowledge from various datasets to create a stronger base model.

Discussion Points:
	•	What is the best way to integrate this “selective loss” mechanism with the current training pipeline?
	•	What experiences have others had with partial supervision in object detection, and are there alternative approaches we should consider?

title: Generalization of model trained on data with sufficient volume but insufficient annotations
body:
Hi, I appreciate you making RF-DETR available.

I want to know if my trainset does not ensure that every target gets annotated in a single image but the total quantity from all images is adequate, how the model generalizes. To be clear, because of the targets' low contrast, like small light gray defects on a white paper, our annotators failed to notice some targets.

Your experience and intuition determine whether I should scrutinize the existing annotations, add more new images, or do both.

Kindly regards,
Noah
author: BotaoPeng98

comments.body:
In my experience, it’s best to do both: re-check your existing annotations and gather more data. Here’s why:

- Missed targets cause confusion for the model, because partial annotations lead to inconsistent training signals. It’s critical that every visible defect—no matter how faint—is annotated.

- Iterative model checks can rapidly spot likely misses or mislabeled areas. Running inference on your dataset helps pinpoint defects the model sees but you didn’t label.

- Low-contrast defects demand consistent guidelines. Define clear thresholds for what counts as a defect so annotators stay uniform in their labeling.

- Adding more data with subtle defects boosts the model’s robustness and recall. The more examples you have of faint patterns, the better the model learns to detect them.
I'm closing the issue for now. Feel free to reopen it if you'll have more questions.

title: Request info on resolution parameter
body: Im not clear if resolution should equal the image size, or if it is a parameter which could be arbitrarily large. Eg. if my image is 560x560 pixels would I get any benefit from resolution=5600?
author: robmarkcole

comments.body:
You would certainly get diminishing returns as you increase size and the model will get slower at first with the square of the size and ultimately with the 4th power of the size as the self attention starts to dominate :) 

The 'right' size is application-specific and is most directly related to your prior on object size. Smaller objects are more easily found in a larger image. 

We train all our models at 560 with a multi resolution augmentation covering up to 840. 

There's research that suggests running at a resolution higher than the native one can be helpful, but is less helpful than having images that are natively higher resolution. 

Does that answer your question?

`Smaller objects are more easily found in a larger image.` - very interesting and not what my intuition would be!

As a rule of thumb then, I should provide images of 560 and use a resolution of 560 for the best results then? I want to eek out all the performance possible

Hey @robmarkcole, thanks for the interesting discussion!

From my experience with other models, a sliding-window approach can really help when you’re dealing with large images and small objects. For example, if you have an image that’s 5600×5600, you could split it into 560×560 patches and run inference on each patch individually. This ensures high resolution for smaller objects without blowing up the model’s memory or compute requirements. It also helps to prep your training data in a similar patch-based way so the model sees consistent input sizes during training.

Hope that adds a useful perspective—definitely not trying to override anything @isaacrob-roboflow mentioned, just sharing what’s worked for me in other setups. Good luck experimenting, and let me know how it goes!

sorry @robmarkcole I meant that, if you have an image at a given size such as 560, scaling up the image and running the model at a higher resolution such as 728 might make it easier to spot small objects than it would be if you were running at 560

I stil don't really understand this. If the model is trained on images at 560, I am better using 560 during inference, or 728 and patching up the image? I think a worked example would be useful. At least for satellite imagery you typically don't want to upscale as this modifies the image properties
The model is trained at a variety of resolutions. 728 will provide higher accuracy, but at the cost of increase latency
Thanks @probicheaux what is the highest resolution I should consider?
@robmarkcole there are diminishing returns for accuracy while increasing latency a lot. You should play around and see what works for your use-case.

title: Object Detection on Live Webcam Feed using RF-DETR
body:
Hi, Can anyone please provide the code to do object detection on live webcam feed using RF-DETR 

Thanks
author: MuhammadMoinFaisal

comments.body:
Hi @MuhammadMoinFaisal 👋🏻 thanks for your interest in RF-DETR. This should work just fine.

```python
import cv2
import supervision as sv
from rfdetr import RFDETRBase
from rfdetr.util.coco_classes import COCO_CLASSES

model = RFDETRBase()

cap = cv2.VideoCapture(0)
while True:
    success, frame = cap.read()
    if not success:
        break

    detections = model.predict(frame, threshold=0.5)
    
    labels = [
        f"{COCO_CLASSES[class_id]} {confidence:.2f}"
        for class_id, confidence
        in zip(detections.class_id, detections.confidence)
    ]

    annotated_frame = frame.copy()
    annotated_frame = sv.BoxAnnotator().annotate(annotated_frame, detections)
    annotated_frame = sv.LabelAnnotator().annotate(annotated_frame, detections, labels)

    cv2.imshow("Webcam", annotated_frame)

    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

cap.release()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()
```
I'm closing the issue. Feel free to reopen if you have more questions. ;)

from tqdm import tqdm
import json

# Define input and output video paths
SOURCE_VIDEO_PATH = "3727445-hd_1920_1080_30fps.mp4"  # Change this to your input video path
TARGET_VIDEO_PATH = "output_video.mp4"  # Change this to your desired output path

# Load class mapping from JSON file
with open("classes.json", "r") as f:
    class_mapping = json.load(f)

# Initialize the RFDETRBase model
model = RFDETRBase()

# Create a generator for video frames
frame_generator = sv.get_video_frames_generator(SOURCE_VIDEO_PATH)

# Get video information (resolution, fps, etc.)
video_info = sv.VideoInfo.from_video_path(SOURCE_VIDEO_PATH)

# Process the video frame by frame
with sv.VideoSink(TARGET_VIDEO_PATH, video_info) as sink:
    for frame in tqdm(frame_generator, desc="Processing video"):
        # Get detections using RFDETRBase model
        detections = model.predict(frame, threshold=0.3)
        
        # Map numeric class IDs to class names for labels
        labels = []
        for class_id in detections.class_id:
            # Convert int to string for dictionary lookup
            class_id_str = str(class_id)
            # Get class name if exists in mapping
            class_name = class_mapping.get(class_id_str)
            labels.append(class_name)
        
        # Create annotated frame
        annotated_frame = frame.copy()
        
        # Apply box annotations
        annotated_frame = sv.BoxAnnotator().annotate(scene=annotated_frame, detections=detections)
        
        # Apply label annotations with proper class names
        annotated_frame = sv.LabelAnnotator(text_thickness=2).annotate(
            scene=annotated_frame, 
            detections=detections,
            labels=labels
        )
        
        # Write the annotated frame to output video
        sink.write_frame(annotated_frame)

print(f"Video processing complete. Output saved to {TARGET_VIDEO_PATH}")

import json

import supervision as sv

model = RFDETRBase()

# Load class mapping from JSON file
with open("classes.json", "r") as f:

class RTSPImageCapture:
    def __init__(self, rtsp_url, output_dir):
        self.rtsp_url = rtsp_url
        self.output_dir = output_dir
        self.cap = None
        self.image_count = 0

    def open_stream(self):
        # Create a VideoCapture object to connect to the RTSP stream
        self.cap = cv2.VideoCapture(self.rtsp_url)

        # Check if the VideoCapture object was successfully created
        if not self.cap.isOpened():
            print("Error: Could not open RTSP stream.")
            exit()

        # Create the output directory if it doesn't exist
        os.makedirs(self.output_dir, exist_ok=True)

    def capture_images(self):
        while True:
            # Capture a frame from the RTSP stream
            ret, frame = self.cap.read()

            # Check if the frame was captured successfully
            if not ret:
                print("Error: Could not read frame from RTSP stream.")
                break
            
            detections =model.predict(frame)
            # Map numeric class IDs to class names for labels
            labels = []
            for class_id in detections.class_id:
                # Convert int to string for dictionary lookup
                class_id_str = str(class_id)
                # Get class name if exists in mapping
                class_name = class_mapping.get(class_id_str)
                labels.append(class_name)

            # Create annotated frame
            annotated_frame = frame.copy()
            
            # Apply box annotations
            annotated_frame = sv.BoxAnnotator().annotate(scene=annotated_frame, detections=detections)

            # Apply label annotations with proper class names
            annotated_frame = sv.LabelAnnotator(text_thickness=2).annotate(
                scene=annotated_frame, 
                detections=detections,
                labels=labels
            )
            # Display the captured frame (optional)
            cv2.imshow('Captured Frame', annotated_frame)

            # Exit the loop when 'q' is pressed
            if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
                break

    def close_stream(self):
        # Release the VideoCapture object and close the OpenCV window
        if self.cap is not None:
            self.cap.release()
            cv2.destroyAllWindows()

    def main(self):
        try:
            self.open_stream()
            self.capture_images()
        finally:
            self.close_stream()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Define the RTSP stream URL and output directory
    rtsp_url = 'rtsp://username:passwd@192.168.1.203:554/stream1'

    # Create an instance of the RTSPImageCapture class
    image_capture = RTSPImageCapture(rtsp_url, output_dir)

    # Run the main function of the class
    image_capture.main()

author: ai8049520

comments.body:
These are great questions and we definitely have more work to do documenting the things you've mentioned.

> I get best model on path "/content/output/checkpoint_best_total.pth" but there is also other candidate for "best" - checkpoint_best_regular.pth and checkpoint_best_ema.pth and checkpoint.pth. Where is best model for best metric value?

During training, we essentially create 2 models -- the regular model that you're training, and another version called the EMA model, which is an average of all model checkpoints. The best regular is saved to `checkpoint_best_regular.pth` and the best EMA is saved to `checkpoint_best_ema.pth`. At the end of training we see who got the all time highest performance on the val set and copy over to `checkpoint_best_total.pth`, so that one should be used for downstream inference.

> How resume from checkpoint
```python
from rfdetr import RFDETRBase
model = RFDETRBase(pretrain_weights="your/pretrain/weights.pth", resume="your/pretrain/weights.pth")
model.train(...)
```

title: Fix weights download if weights are not properly downloaded
body:
# Description

If you stop weights download during the download step, RF-DETR returns:

```python
Loading pretrain weights
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/Users/james/rf-detr-launch/rfdetr/main.py", line 57, in __init__
    checkpoint = torch.load(args.pretrain_weights, map_location='cpu', weights_only=False)
  File "/Users/james/rf-detr-launch/venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/torch/serialization.py", line 1432, in load
    with _open_zipfile_reader(opened_file) as opened_zipfile:
         ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/Users/james/rf-detr-launch/venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/torch/serialization.py", line 763, in __init__
    super().__init__(torch._C.PyTorchFileReader(name_or_buffer))
                     ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
RuntimeError: PytorchStreamReader failed reading zip archive: failed finding central directory
```

This PR fixes the bug by attempting to re-download the weights if `pytorch` is unable to open the file.

With this change, a user will now see:

```
Failed to load pretrain weights, re-downloading
rf-detr-base.pth:  96%|███████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████▊    | 341M/355M [00:59<00:02,
```

You can test this change by starting a training job without the base weights locally, pressing Ctrl-C during download, then trying to run your train script again.

title: image classification model ?
body: Do you have any plans to develop an image classification model similar to the YOLO-cls models ?
author: Tahirc1

comments.body: We currently have no intention of doing that. I would recommend using a devoted image classification model such as a ViT or even a resnet instead of using an adaptation of an object detector to classification.
We use DINOv2 to get our transfer to novel domains so if you're looking for a classifier similar to RF-DETR in behavior I'd just use that model as your starting point :)
